evidence.claim: The FY 2022 deficit fell to $1.375 trillion, was half of FY 2021, $1.8 trillion lower than the deficit the President inherited, and the economy had added more than 10 million jobs with unemployment back to 3.5 percent.
evidence.title: Joint Statement of Janet L. Yellen, Secretary of the Treasury, and Shalanda D. Young, Director of the Office of Management and Budget, on Budget Results for Fiscal Year 2022
evidence.excerpt: The FY 2022 deficit fell to $1.375 trillion, was half of FY 2021, $1.8 trillion lower than the deficit the President inherited, and the economy had added more than 10 million jobs with unemployment back to 3.5 percent.
evidence.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The 2022 deficit of $1.375 trillion...' and the following paragraph on jobs
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary Treasury/OMB statement with concrete fiscal and labor-market figures; strong for outcome context and administration attribution, though some claims are self-described.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Biden’s administration and fiscal agenda; the budget result is not purely his personal action but is directly tied to executive leadership.
contrary_evidence: Treasury’s own framing mixes inherited recovery effects with administration choices, so attribution is partial rather than exclusive.

evidence.claim: The CPI-U rose 6.5 percent over the 12 months ending December 2022, while the index for all items less food and energy rose 5.7 percent and shelter rose 7.5 percent.
evidence.title: Consumer Price Index News Release - 2022 M12 Results
evidence.excerpt: The CPI-U rose 6.5 percent over the 12 months ending December 2022, while the index for all items less food and energy rose 5.7 percent and shelter rose 7.5 percent.
evidence.source_locator: paragraphs around the 'The all items index increased 6.5 percent...' and 'The index for all items less food and energy rose 5.7 percent...' lines
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary statistical release from BLS; direct, authoritative inflation evidence for the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Contextual rather than fully attributable to Biden, because much of inflation was driven by pandemic, supply-chain, and energy shocks.
contrary_evidence: High inflation is a major negative for household welfare and a constraint on economic stewardship.

evidence.claim: Real average hourly earnings for all employees decreased 1.7 percent from December 2021 to December 2022.
evidence.title: Real Earnings News Release - 2022 M12 Results
evidence.excerpt: Real average hourly earnings for all employees decreased 1.7 percent from December 2021 to December 2022.
evidence.source_locator: table A-1 and the opening summary of the real earnings release
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary BLS release using CPI deflation and standard earnings series; strong household purchasing-power evidence.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This reflects national real-wage conditions under Biden, but not a policy fully under presidential control because inflation and wage setting were partly outside the White House.
contrary_evidence: Monthly nominal earnings rose, but inflation outpaced them over the year.

evidence.claim: Total nonfarm payroll employment increased by 223,000 in December 2022, the unemployment rate edged down to 3.5 percent, and payroll employment rose by 4.5 million over the year.
evidence.title: Employment Situation News Release - 2022 M13 Results
evidence.excerpt: Total nonfarm payroll employment increased by 223,000 in December 2022, the unemployment rate edged down to 3.5 percent, and payroll employment rose by 4.5 million over the year.
evidence.source_locator: opening summary of the December 2022 Employment Situation release
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary BLS labor-market release; direct and standard source for jobs and unemployment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly attributable to the broader U.S. economy and administration policies, but not uniquely to Biden alone.
contrary_evidence: Strong employment data do not erase inflation and real-income pressure.

evidence.claim: The IMF said the United States had staged a strong recovery, unemployment had returned to end-2019 levels, output was close to its pre-pandemic trend, and inflation had accelerated broadly beyond food and energy.
evidence.title: United States: 2022 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for the United States
evidence.excerpt: The IMF said the United States had staged a strong recovery, unemployment had returned to end-2019 levels, output was close to its pre-pandemic trend, and inflation had accelerated broadly beyond food and energy.
evidence.source_locator: summary section on the IMF country report page
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent multilateral surveillance source with direct 2022 assessment; strong for macro context, weaker for direct policy attribution.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is primarily country-level and partly attributable to Biden’s administration through fiscal policy, but the IMF explicitly treats the Fed, global shocks, and prior pandemic support as key drivers too.
contrary_evidence: The IMF’s positive recovery language is paired with a warning that inflation was already creating hardship and needed tighter monetary policy.

evidence.claim: CBO estimated that enacting the Inflation Reduction Act would reduce deficits by $90 billion over 2022-2031.
evidence.title: Estimated Budgetary Effects of H.R. 5376, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022
evidence.excerpt: CBO estimated that enacting the Inflation Reduction Act would reduce deficits by $90 billion over 2022-2031.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary budget scorekeeping from Congress’s nonpartisan budget office; directly relevant to fiscal stewardship.
evidence.period_fit: In-period legislative estimate for Biden’s 2022 signature initiative.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Biden’s legislative push and signing, though the enacted bill reflects congressional bargaining.
contrary_evidence: CBO’s estimate is about deficit effect, not a complete welfare or inflation verdict.

evidence.claim: Biden said the law would lower prescription-drug costs and health premiums, invest $369 billion in clean energy and energy security, create tens of thousands of good-paying jobs, and cut deficits over the next decade.
evidence.title: Remarks on Signing Legislation To Combat Inflation, Promote Clean Energy Production, and Reduce Prescription Drug Costs
evidence.excerpt: Biden said the law would lower prescription-drug costs and health premiums, invest $369 billion in clean energy and energy security, create tens of thousands of good-paying jobs, and cut deficits over the next decade.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary presidential signing remarks with specific policy claims; strong for intent and enactment, weaker for realized effects in 2022.
evidence.period_fit: Exactly in-period and tied to one of the central 2022 economic laws.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct presidential action and advocacy by Biden.
contrary_evidence: The economic effects were mostly prospective in 2022 and not yet fully observable that year.

evidence.claim: The White House said the CHIPS implementation order would lower the cost of goods, create high-paying manufacturing jobs, and make critical technologies at home.
evidence.title: FACT SHEET: President Biden Signs Executive Order to Implement the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022
evidence.excerpt: The White House said the CHIPS implementation order would lower the cost of goods, create high-paying manufacturing jobs, and make critical technologies at home.
evidence.source_locator: fact sheet text around the implementation goals
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary executive-branch fact sheet; strong for policy direction and implementation architecture, weaker for realized outcomes within 2022.
evidence.period_fit: In-period and directly tied to Biden’s 2022 industrial policy.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Biden through presidential order and administration direction.
contrary_evidence: Implementation benefits were prospective in 2022 and depended on later execution and private investment.

evidence.claim: Commerce said the CHIPS program would revitalize domestic semiconductor manufacturing, spur innovation, and create tens of thousands of good-paying manufacturing jobs and more than 100,000 construction jobs, including pathways for women, people of color, veterans, and rural workers.
evidence.title: Biden Administration Releases Implementation Strategy for $50 Billion CHIPS for America program
evidence.excerpt: Commerce said the CHIPS program would revitalize domestic semiconductor manufacturing, spur innovation, and create tens of thousands of good-paying manufacturing jobs and more than 100,000 construction jobs, including pathways for women, people of color, veterans, and rural workers.
evidence.source_locator: implementation strategy summary and goal bullets
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary departmental implementation strategy with concrete job and inclusion targets; strong evidence of policy design and delegated execution.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and immediately after the CHIPS Act became law.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Biden’s administration, though execution was delegated to Commerce.
contrary_evidence: The strategy describes projected jobs and inclusion, not completed outcomes in 2022.

evidence.claim: Transportation Secretary Buttigieg said the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law’s bridge investment was the largest dedicated bridge investment since the Interstate Highway System and that the law would improve supply chains, daily travel, and create jobs.
evidence.title: Implementation of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act by the U.S. Department of Transportation
evidence.excerpt: Transportation Secretary Buttigieg said the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law’s bridge investment was the largest dedicated bridge investment since the Interstate Highway System and that the law would improve supply chains, daily travel, and create jobs.
evidence.source_locator: March 2, 2022 Senate testimony, especially the bridge-investment and jobs paragraphs
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary departmental testimony with concrete program details; credible for implementation and spending, less direct for whole-economy effects.
evidence.period_fit: In-period and directly about 2022 implementation of Biden’s infrastructure agenda.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Biden’s administration through enacted law and delegated implementation.
contrary_evidence: The testimony speaks to planned and underway projects, not complete macro outcomes in 2022.

evidence.claim: Real median household income fell for White households, real median earnings fell 2.2 percent for all workers, the official poverty rate was 11.5 percent, and the SPM rose to 12.4 percent as temporary Child Tax Credit, EITC, and stimulus expansions expired.
evidence.title: Income, Poverty and Health Insurance Coverage in the United States: 2022
evidence.excerpt: Real median household income fell for White households, real median earnings fell 2.2 percent for all workers, the official poverty rate was 11.5 percent, and the SPM rose to 12.4 percent as temporary Child Tax Credit, EITC, and stimulus expansions expired.
evidence.source_locator: earnings and poverty sections, especially the highlighted bullets and the paragraphs around lines 198-199 and 227-243
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary Census publication with standard income, poverty, and distribution metrics; strong for household-welfare context, though retrospective.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is only partly attributable to Biden because the deterioration reflects the end of temporary pandemic-relief policies, inflation, and household distribution effects beyond direct presidential control.
contrary_evidence: The report also shows some groups, including Black households, saw the official poverty rate improve, so the distributional picture is mixed.

unresolved_gaps: No direct 2022 evidence on command-and-control or custody changes beyond declaratory policy and reactive crisis signaling.
Limited direct evidence on internal U.S.-Ukraine operational restrictions and private bargaining with Russia.
Weak direct evidence on federal prison/detention conditions and on whether the listed reforms materially reduced abuse in 2022.
Little direct evidence on electoral manipulation, subnational election protection outcomes, or media/platform pressure beyond speeches and DOJ initiatives.
Direct evidence on appointment quality and empowered economic professionals is thinner than the policy and macro-outcome record.
Outcome evidence is strong on access and targeted relief, but weaker on durable, independent measurement of household welfare change within 2022.
No direct 2022 forensic finding, ethics violation, or investigative record tying Joe Biden personally to self-dealing, concealment, or family benefit.
Appointment and patronage evidence around Biden's own circle remains thin.
Much of the evidence is still program-design and rollout architecture rather than completed, award-level implementation output.
